title: How air flows through a bird
caption: Birds breathe with balloon-like air sacs that pump air through stiff lungs, so fresh air flows through the lungs in the same direction when the bird breathes in and when it breathes out. That steady stream of air is what powers a bird's voice.
author: L. Shyamal (based on R. McNeill Alexander, Animals)
credit: Bird respiration diagram by L. Shyamal, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).
modified: Removed editor metadata, added a viewBox so it scales, added sans-serif font fallback; drawing unchanged.

title: A bird's air sacs
caption: Besides its lungs, a bird has a set of thin-walled air sacs that fill much of its body and even reach into some bones. They act like bellows, storing and pushing the air that a bird sings with.
author: C. Abraczinskas (from Sereno et al. 2008, PLoS ONE 3(9): e3303)
credit: Air sac diagram by C. Abraczinskas, from Sereno et al. (2008) PLoS ONE 3(9): e3303, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5.
modified: Kept English labels only (removed French language layer), removed editor metadata and embedded SVG fonts, added sans-serif font fallback.

title: The syrinx: a bird's voice box
caption: Birds make sound with a syrinx, found deep in the chest where the windpipe splits into the two bronchi, not in the throat like our larynx. Thin membranes in its walls vibrate as air rushes past, a bit like the reed of a clarinet.
author: Uwe Gille
credit: Syrinx schematic by Uwe Gille, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

title: Inside a blackbird's syrinx (1900)
caption: A slice through the syrinx of a male blackbird, with the windpipe at the top and the two bronchi below. The thin membranes and soft lips on each side are where the sound starts, and the muscles alongside tighten or loosen them to change the note.
author: Valentin Häcker
credit: Valentin Häcker, Der Gesang der Vögel: seine anatomischen und biologischen Grundlagen (Jena: Gustav Fischer, 1900), Fig. 2, p. 5. Public domain; scan via Biodiversity Heritage Library / Internet Archive (MBLWHOI Library).

title: A simple syrinx: tyrant flycatcher (1900)
caption: The syrinx of a ruddy-tailed flycatcher, a perching bird that is not a true songbird, has just one simple pair of muscles running down each side. Compare it with the crow's syrinx, where many small muscles give songbirds much finer control over their voice.
author: Valentin Häcker (after Johannes Müller)
credit: Valentin Häcker, Der Gesang der Vögel: seine anatomischen und biologischen Grundlagen (Jena: Gustav Fischer, 1900), Fig. 5 (after J. Müller), p. 10. Public domain; scan via Biodiversity Heritage Library / Internet Archive (MBLWHOI Library).

legend: tr.br. tracheobronchial muscle; st.t. sternotracheal muscle

title: A songbird's syrinx muscles: carrion crow (1900)
caption: Crows are songbirds, and their syrinx is wrapped in several pairs of small muscles; here the outer layer has been removed to show the deeper ones. Each side can be controlled separately, which is how some songbirds sing two notes at once.
author: Valentin Häcker
credit: Valentin Häcker, Der Gesang der Vögel: seine anatomischen und biologischen Grundlagen (Jena: Gustav Fischer, 1900), Fig. 9, p. 13. Public domain; scan via Biodiversity Heritage Library / Internet Archive (MBLWHOI Library).
